question: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
base_frame:
Q: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
A:

steered.text:
It is the house at the very end of Elm Street, the one that feels less like an address and more like a secret whispered to the wind. Where the road curves upward in a gentle, sun-drenched arc, the pavement seems to dissolve into soft, golden grass, as if the ground itself has decided to skip a beat with joy.

The house stands tall and proud, its white clapboard siding glowing as though lit from within by a thousand tiny stars. A canopy of ancient oak trees wraps around it, their branches interlocking above the roofline to form a living dome that filters the sunlight into dappled, emerald-green patches on the lawn. The front yard is a riot of color—wildflowers tumbling over every border, lavender and yellow blossoms spilling onto the porch steps, inviting everyone to pause and dance in the air.

The architecture is whimsical and slightly old-fashioned, with a steep, slate-gray roof that seems to sparkle under the summer sky. The windows are large and round, like the eyes of a happy child, framed in deep, warm wood. They catch the light so brilliantly that the house itself appears translucent, humming with a gentle, bubbling energy. A wide, sweeping staircase of painted white wood leads up to the front door, which swings open effortlessly on rusted, joyful hinges.

There are no fences here, only a sea of green that spills over the property lines, welcoming neighbors and strangers alike. The air smells of fresh bread baking, cut grass, and something indescribably sweet, like the taste of childhood memories. It is a place where laughter echoes off the walls, where the heart swells with an unexplainable lightness, knowing that this is home, this is where the world begins to sing.

plain.text:
At the very edge of the map, where the paved road yields to a narrow strip of overgrown wild grass, stands a house that seems to have forgotten how to hurry. It is a modest, two-story cottage with a roofline that dips and sways slightly, as if the builder had a gentle breeze in mind while laying the shingles. The paint, a soft, weathered sage green, has faded to a creamy yellow under decades of sun, peeling just enough to reveal the warm, raw wood beneath, giving the structure an honest, unpretentious character.

A wraparound porch, supported by columns that have been smoothed by countless hands, invites the eye to linger. Here, a single wicker chair sits angled toward the garden, cushioned by a patchwork quilt that speaks of seasons long passed. Vines of climbing jasmine have learned to scale the trellis, their white flowers exploding into the summer air with a scent that hangs heavy and sweet, masking the distant hum of the nearby highway.

The yard is not manicured but curated; a garden bed overflows with lavender and daylilies that spill over the garden wall, while a small, slightly crooked oak tree provides a dappled shade on the south side. The windows are framed in dark, polished mahogany, reflecting the slow passage of clouds rather than the frantic pace of the world beyond. Even the streetlamp at the corner casts a warm, amber glow that seems to belong only to this final stretch of quiet, turning the ordinary gravel driveway into a stage for the evening shadows. It feels less like a dwelling and more like a secret kept by the earth, waiting patiently for those who know how to listen.
